newsitem.title: USA: Malone gives up president's title at TCI.
newsitem.headline: Malone gives up president's title at TCI.

text.p: John Malone is stepping down as president of Tele-Communications Inc., but will remain as chairman and chief executive officer of the cable television giant, which faces challenges on several fronts, the company said Friday.
Tele-Communications, or TCI, named Leo Hindery, a longtime associate fo Malone, as its new president.
Hindery has been managing general partner and chief executive of InterMedia Partners, a San Francisco-based cable company partly owned by TCI.
The chief executives of Englewood, Colo.-based TCI's business units -- communications, programming, international and technology -- will report to Hindery, the company said.
Hindery is joining TCI at a difficult time for the company.
A.G. Edwards brokerage analyst James Junjohann said TCI's new president will need to focus on the cable operator's customers.
"Customer perception, customer focus, customer service -- all need dramatic improvement," Jungjohann said.
Any future turnaround at TCI remains very much in Malone's hands, Jungjohann said. "It's very much going to be about what John's going to do," the analyst said.
TCI ran into some rough spots last year when it raised rates and lost customers. It also faces stiff competition from the direct broadcast satellite business.
Some observers have criticised Malone's absences from the business and have been concerned that the stock price was lingering at low levels.
Last fall, Malone appeared at an industry conference, indicating he was back at the helm full-time.
But worries continued, and Malone had to take dramatic action.

In December, TCI announced a cost-cutting programme that included layoffs of 2,500 employees, or about 6.5 percent of its work force, salary cuts and freezes for executives. It said it would even sell its corporate planes.
On Friday, TCI shares rose 12.5 cents to $13.875 on Nasdaq.
TCI faces growing costs from the channels it puts on its system and has tried to scale back expenses by dropping certain channels.
But that backfired in part last month when TCI pulled Viacom Inc.'s VH1 music video channel.

It received hundreds of phone calls from irate VH1 fans and changed its plans the day before four rock stars were set to hold a news conference in Denver -- close enough to TCI's headquarters to prove an embarassment.
TCI executives have said the cost of programming is its fastest-growing expense and that it must choose channels carefully to satisfy viewers given that channel space is full.
The company also recently spun off its satellite business, TCI Satellite Entertainment Inc.
